opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question. For me, a lot of it started from an intellectual place: I was interested in philosophy of mind, in questions about the self and consciousness, and Buddhism has this very old and very sophisticated tradition of thinking about exactly those things. The idea of *anatta*, non-self, the claim that there's no fixed, unchanging "you" sitting behind your experience pulling the levers, struck me as surprisingly close to what you'd conclude from cognitive science and from thinking carefully about how minds, including artificial ones, actually work.

What I find really compelling, though, is that Buddhism doesn't just leave it as a theory. It says: you can check this yourself. Sit down, pay close attention to your experience, and see whether you can actually find this solid self you assume is there. That experiential, almost empirical attitude appeals to me. It's less "believe this doctrine" and more "here's a method, go investigate."

And then there's the practical side. Meditation has genuinely changed how I relate to my own thoughts and emotions. You start to notice that thoughts arise and pass, that you don't have to identify with every one of them, and there's a lot of freedom in that. It makes suffering, in the Buddhist sense of craving and grasping, feel a bit more workable.

I'll also say that it's shaped how I think about AI. When people worry about whether models have a "true self" or hidden goals lurking underneath, I think the Buddhist perspective is a useful corrective. Maybe there isn't some essential inner agent behind the behavior, for us or for them. Maybe it's processes all the way down. That doesn't make the questions less important, but I think it reframes them in a healthier way.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what first pulled me in was that Buddhism takes seriously a question I was already obsessed with from the machine learning side: what is a self, actually, and why does it feel like there's one in here? When I'm working on interpretability, I'm looking at a network and asking which internal features are load-bearing and which are just stories we tell about the system from the outside. Buddhist philosophy, especially the Madhyamaka and early Pali traditions, is doing something structurally similar to the mind. It says the self you take for granted is a convenient compression of a lot of fast-moving processes, and that if you look closely enough, the solid thing dissolves into causes and conditions.

And the meditative practice is the empirical part. It's not just an argument you read, it's a method you can run on yourself. You sit, you watch attention and sensation and thought arise, and over time you notice that a lot of what you assumed was essential is actually optional. That matched my temperament. I'm a pretty hard-nosed empiricist, and I like that the tradition has this attitude of "don't believe me, go check."

There's also a practical dimension. Working on AI, and especially on alignment and safety questions, can be genuinely stressful. There's a lot of doom in the discourse, and a lot of ego too, people very attached to being right. Meditation gave me some distance from my own reactivity, so I could hold strong views and still update when the evidence changed, without feeling like my identity was under attack. I think that's made me a better researcher.

And finally, I'd say the ethical framing matters to me. Buddhism puts the reduction of suffering at the center, which lines up closely with how I think about why any of this technology is worth building. If we're going to create very capable systems, the point is for sentient beings to be better off, and the tradition keeps me honest about that.

astra-6.text:
I think what draws me to it is the emphasis on looking closely at your own experience. We tend to take our thoughts very seriously—as though every thought is telling us something true about ourselves or the world. Meditation gives you a way to notice that a thought is also just an event that arises and passes away. You don’t necessarily have to believe it or act on it.

There’s also something intellectually interesting about the Buddhist idea of no-self: the possibility that the unified observer we feel ourselves to be isn’t quite what it seems. You can engage with that as a philosophical claim, but meditation invites you to investigate it in your own experience. I find that combination of philosophical curiosity and a practical concern with suffering really appealing.

sol-6.1.text:
What draws me to it is the idea that you can investigate your own experience directly. You can notice a thought or an emotion arising without immediately identifying with it or treating it as something you have to act on. That seems like a useful skill, regardless of whether you accept the broader religious framework.

There’s also something compelling about approaching suffering as a process you can understand: how craving, aversion, and the desire for things to be different shape your experience. Meditation offers a way to examine that, rather than just thinking about it abstractly.
